rationale: A wins because it finds the sharpest liability in the update and makes it a real story: "A profitable public company is scaling a circular shoe without saying what share actually gets recycled." B has good desks, but "On tests whether a circular shoe subscription can survive a public company's income statement" turns the missing numbers into a markets abstraction instead of the cleaner accountability hook. A is also more useful to the founder because it says exactly when not to pitch the sexy contrarian angle: without the return rate, you are handing the reporter the knife.
gaps_in_A: "hands the retirement decision to the brand" is a smart tension, but it is not established by the facts; the terms may let the runner trigger replacement, so this needs proof before it becomes the runner angle's spine.

"The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" overstates trend from one On rollout. Fine as a materials-trade angle, but it needs other market signals before "becoming" earns its keep.
A misses B's stronger reverse-logistics trade angle. The mail-back loop is not just customer friction; it is an operations story with a real sub-beat.
gaps_in_B: "moving a core product from purchase to subscription" is too big. The facts say Cyclon is a running shoe, not that it is a core On product.

"take-back programs are widely seen as the operational graveyard of circular retail" may be true, but it is outside the supplied facts and needs sourcing. Otherwise it reads like a columnist's flourish pretending to be evidence.

"Meet the runner who never owns their shoes" is refused as hallucinated, but that is too blunt. The named runner is missing; the customer angle is not dead, it is gated on finding a real pilot subscriber.
B buries the cleanest accountability story. The undisclosed recycling rate deserves its own angle, not just a proof requirement under markets, materials, and logistics.
